Suppose we are given a system of linear equations and its respective augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}-{x}_{3} &=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}+4{x}_{3} &=-2 \\ 5{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3} &=1\end{aligned}
$$

We can apply some operations to the augmented matrix that do not change the set of solutions for the corresponding system. These operations are called **elementary row operations**. 

After applying an **elementary row operation** to the augmented matrix, the new corresponding system will have the same solutions.

There are three types of elementary row operations:

- switching any two rows: 

$$
R_i \leftrightarrow R_j
$$

- multiplying (each element of) a row by a non-zero number: 

$$
R_i := k R_i,\qquad k \neq 0
$$

- adding a multiple of one row to another row: 

$$
R_j := R_j+k R_i,\qquad j \neq i
$$

In the notations above, the "$:=$" symbol is called the **assignment operator.** We use this to assign new values to every element of a given row.

For example, the row operation $R_1 := 2 R_1$ means, "create a new row $1$ by taking the old row $1$ and multiplying it by $2.$" When we do this, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 3 & -1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 4 & -2 \\ 5 & 1 & 1 & 1\end{array}\right]\,{R}_{1}:=2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}2\cdot 1 & 2\cdot 3 & 2\cdot (-1) & 2\cdot 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 4 & -2 \\ 5 & 1 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}2 & 6 & -2 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 4 & -2 \\ 5 & 1 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

A few final points on notation.

- We use the similarity symbol ($\sim$) to indicate when one matrix is transformed into another matrix using elementary row operations.

- The assignment operator $:=$ is sometimes called the "walrus operator" because it looks like a walrus on its side!

Consider the following system of linear equations and its respective **augmented matrix**:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2x+6y &=-2 \\ 3x-y &=2\end{aligned}\right.
$$

$$
M =
	\left[
	\begin{array}{cc|c}2 & 6 & -2 \\ 3 & -1 & 2\end{array}
	\right]
$$

If we can convert the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form, then we can solve the system using back substitution.

The procedure for reducing $M$ to row echelon form using elementary row operations is called **Gaussian elimination**. To perform Gaussian elimination on a $2 \times 2$ matrix, we use the following procedure.

**Step 1:** Consider the entry $a_{11}=2$ of the coefficient matrix. This entry is called a **pivot element**. We want to make this entry equal to $1$. So, the first elementary row operation will be 

$$
R_1 := \dfrac{1}{2}R_1
$$

and we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}2 & 6 & -2 \\ 3 & -1 & 2\end{array}\right] & {R}_{1}:=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 & -1 \\ 3 & -1 & 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2:** Consider the entry $a_{21}=3$ below the first pivot element. We want to make this entry equal to $0$. So, the second elementary row operation will be 

$$
R_2 :=R_2+(-3)R_1
$$

and we have

$$
\begin{aligned} & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}{\color{red}1} & 3 & -1 \\ {\color{blue}3} & -1 & 2\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+({\color{blue}-3}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}{\color{red}1} & 3 & -1 \\ {\color{blue}0} & -10 & 5\end{array}\right].\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3:** Finally, consider the entry $a_{22}=-10$. This entry is the second pivot element, and we would like to make it equal to $1$. So, the third elementary row operation will be 

$$
R_2 :=\dfrac{1}{-10}R_2
$$

and we get $M$ in row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 3 & -1 \\ 0 & {\color{red}-10} & 5\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2}:=\frac{1}{{\color{red}-10}}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 3 & -1 \\ 0 & {\color{red}1} & -\frac{1}{2}\end{array}\right].\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+3y &=-1 \\ y &=-\frac{1}{2},\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $y=-\dfrac{1}{2}$ tells us the value of $y.$ Substituting this value into the first equation, we get

$$
x+3 \left( -\dfrac{1}{2} \right) = -1 
	\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
	x=\dfrac{1}{2}.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=\dfrac{1}{2}$ and $y=-\dfrac{1}{2}.$ Or, in vector form, $$
\displaystyle \left< \dfrac{1}{2}, -\dfrac{1}{2} \right>.
$$

We need to solve the system of equations consisting of the two lines:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+2y &=1 \\ 2x-y &=7\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We will use the elimination method to solve the system. Notice that if we multiply the second equation by $2,$ then we will get a $-2y$ term that can cancel with the $2y$ term in the first equation:



$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+2y &=1 && \\ 2x-y &=7 && |\:\times 2\end{aligned}\right. \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \left\{\begin{aligned}x+2y &=1 \\ 4x-2y &=14\end{aligned}\right.
$$



Adding the two equations eliminates the $y$-variable and allows us to solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x+\cancel{2y} & =1 \\ 4x-\cancel{2y} & =14 \\ (x+4x) & =(1+14) \\ 5x & =15 \\ x & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can substitute $x=3$ into the equation $x+2y=1$ to solve for $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2y & =1 \\ 3+2y & =1 \\ 2y & =-2 \\ y & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system is $x=3, \, y=-1.$ So the coordinates of the point of intersection are $(3,-1).$

The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L = \int _a^b \sqrt{1 + [f'(x)]^2} \, \textrm{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)= x^{3/2},$ $a=0,$ and $b=\dfrac{4}{3}.$

First, we find the derivative of $f(x)\mathbin{:}$

$$
f'(x) =   \dfrac{3}{2}x^{1/2}
$$

$$

A **permutation** is a selection of objects in which order matters. Two selections of the same items are counted as different selections if they are in a different order.

For example, suppose that we have $5$ books, but our bookshelf can only hold $3.$ We want to place $3$ books on the shelf and the rest will stay in the drawer. 

How many permutations are there? In other words, how many ways can we place $3$ books on the shelf (in a particular order)?

Let's think about all the choices we have as we fill up the bookshelf:

- We can place any of our $5$ books in the first slot of the bookshelf.

- Now that we've placed one book on the bookshelf, we have $4$ books remaining. We can place any of these $4$ remaining books in the second slot.

- Now that we've placed two books on the bookshelf, we have $3$ books remaining. We can place any of these $3$ remaining books in the third slot.

The number of choices we have for each slot is shown below:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{5 choices} & \text{4 choices} & \text{3 choices}\end{aligned}
$$

To find the total number of arrangements, we can use the multiplication principle:

$$
5\times4\times3 = 60.
$$

Suppose that we want to solve, *without using graphs*, the following system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y &=1 \\ 5x-y &=11\end{aligned}\right.
$$

To solve the system, we must combine the equations into a single equation that can be solved using algebraic manipulation. One way to combine the equations is to use the **elimination method.** 

Notice that the coefficient of $y$ in the first equation is $1,$ and the coefficient of $y$ in the second equation is $-1.$ Since these numbers add to zero, we can *add* the two equations, *eliminate* the variable $y,$ and solve the resulting equation for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}x+\cancel{y} & =1 \\ 5x-\cancel{y} & =11 \\ (x+5x) & =(1+11) \\ 6x & =12 \\ x & =2\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solution must have $x=2.$ However, we still need to find $y.$ To do this, we substitute $x=2$ back into one of the equations. Let's choose the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}x+y & =1 \\ (2)+y & =1 \\ y & =-1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x=2$ and $y=-1,$ which can be expressed as $(2, -1).$

$$
(A - \lambda I) \textbf{x}=\mathbf{0}.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =2.$ So, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =\begin{bmatrix}7 & -4 \\ 5 & -2\end{bmatrix}-2\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5 & -4 \\ 5 & -4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A - \lambda I) \textbf{x}=\mathbf{0}.
$$

With that in mind, let's consider each of the eigenvalues separately. 

- For $\lambda =1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 0 & -4\end{bmatrix}-1\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 0 & -5\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

We have to solve the corresponding system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2} &=0 \\ -5{x}_{2} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -5 & 0\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-5){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $2$nd one). So, $x_1$ is a free variable. 
From the first equation, we obtain  $x_2=0.$ Therefore, the general solution is
$$
{\left[ \begin{array}{c}{x}_{1} \\ 0\end{array} \right]},
	\qquad x_1 \in \mathbb{R}.
$$
Setting, for instance, $x_1=1,$ we get the eigenvector 
$$
\mathbf{v}_1 = \displaystyle{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}1 \\ 0\end{array} \right]}}.
$$

- For $\lambda =-4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 0 & -4\end{bmatrix}-(-4)\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

We have to solve the corresponding system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}5{x}_{1}-{x}_{2} &=0 \\ 0 &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}5 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right]\end{aligned}
$$

In the matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). So, $x_2$ is a free variable. 
From the first equation, we obtain $x_1=\dfrac{1}{5}x_2.$ Therefore, the general solution is
$$
{\left[ \begin{array}{c}{\displaystyle \frac{1}{5}} {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{array} \right]},
	\quad x_2 \in \mathbb{R}.
$$
Setting, for instance, $x_2=5,$ we get the eigenvector 
$$
\mathbf{v}_2 = \displaystyle{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}1 \\ 5\end{array} \right]}}.
$$

Therefore, two linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix $A$ are
$$
{\left[ \begin{array}{c}1 \\ 0\end{array} \right]}, {\left[ \begin{array}{c}1 \\ 5\end{array} \right]}.
$$

The matrix $M$ is already in row echelon form, but we can transform it even further into the **reduced row echelon form** (RREF) using the standard **Gauss-Jordan** method. 

The algorithm is similar to the algorithm of converting a matrix to row echelon form, except that we need to make *all* the pivot entries equal to $1$ and *all* the entries below *and above* a pivot (in a pivot column) equal to $0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :=-\frac{1}{2}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The final matrix is in reduced row echelon form:

- all the pivot entries are equal to $1$ (here we have $\color{red}1$'s on the main diagonal), and

- all the entries below and above a pivot are equal to ${\color{blue}0}.$

Sometimes, we might have a system of equations with fractional coefficients, such as the following:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{5}{4}y=-4 \\ 7x-5y=-2\end{aligned}
$$

We can turn the system into an equivalent system involving only integer coefficients. This will make it easier to solve.

In general, we multiply each equation by its lowest common denominator. In this instance, multiplying the first equation by the lowest common denominator of the fractions $(4)$ will do the job:

$$
{\left\{  \begin{array}{ll}{\displaystyle \frac{1}{ {\color{red}2}}} x + {\displaystyle \frac{5}{ {\color{red}4}}} y = - 4 & {\color{blue}| \hspace{0.222em} \times  4} \\ 7 x - 5 y = - 2 & \end{array} \right. }
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
{\left\{  \begin{array}{l}2 x + 5 y = - 16 \\ 7 x - 5 y = - 2\end{array} \right. }
$$

Now, we can solve the system using, for example, the elimination method. Notice that the $5y$ term in the first equation can cancel with the $-5y$ term in the second equation.

Adding the two equations eliminates the $y$-variable, and allows us to solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+\cancel{5y} & =-16 \\ 7x-\cancel{5y} & =-2 \\ 9x & =-18 \\ x & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can substitute $x=-2$ into the equation $7x - 5y= -2$ to solve for $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}7x-5y & =-2 \\ 7(-2)-5y & =-2 \\ -14-5y & =-2 \\ -5y & =12 \\ y & =-\frac{12}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x=-2, \,y=-\dfrac{12}{5}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =x-1 \\ \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \text{d}u & =\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

 **Step 2**: Calculate the new limits.

$$

$$

while the upper limit $x=2$ becomes

$$

$$

The corresponding system is now


$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-y+z &=2 \\ 0x+y-3z &=-5 \\ 0x+0y+0z &=0.\end{aligned}\right.

$$

$$

- $m_{22}=1,$ which is the coefficient of $y.$

Each elementary matrix $E$ is invertible, and the corresponding inverse is always an elementary matrix of the same type as $E$.

$$
[{\color{blue}{E}}\, |\, {\color{red}I_2}]	
=

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}[E\,|\,{I}_{2}] & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 4 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} &  & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-4){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -4 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =[{I}_{2}\,|\,{E}^{-1}]\end{aligned}

$$

$$

Suppose we want to find the inverse of the matrix 

$$
A = {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 7\end{array} \right]}.
$$ 

We can compute the inverse of $A$ using elementary row operations. There are two key advantages to using row operations to compute the inverse of a matrix:

- The method works for any invertible matrix of any size, not just $2\times 2$ matrices.

- It requires significantly less computation than some alternative methods. This is especially true for large matrices.

Here, we'll focus on the $2\times 2$ case. We use the following fact:

*The row operations that transform $A$ into the identity matrix $I_2$ also transform $I_2$ into $A^{-1}$*.

So, to find the inverse of $A,$ we proceed as follows:

**Step 1:** Write down $\color{blue}A$ and the identity matrix $I_2$ side-by-side, as shown below:
$$
[{\color{blue}{A}}\, |\, {\color{black}I_2}]	
=	
\left[{\begin{array}{cc|cc}{\color{blue}1} & {\color{blue}2} & 1 & 0 \\ {\color{blue}3} & {\color{blue}7} & 0 & 1\end{array}}\right]
$$

**Step 2:** Apply the standard Gauss-Jordan method to transform the matrix $A$ into the identity matrix. We perform the same row operations on both matrices:

$$
\begin{aligned}[A\,|\,{I}_{2}\,] & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 7 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 7 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =[\,I\,|\,{A}^{-1}]\end{aligned}
$$

The matrix $A^{-1}$ is obtained on the right-hand side of our big matrix after the transformation. Therefore, 

$$
A^{-1} = {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}7 & - 2 \\ - 3 & 1\end{array} \right]}.
$$

$$

$$

One nice property of block diagonal matrices is that we can calculate their determinants relatively easily.

To compute the determinant of a block diagonal matrix, we simply calculate the product of the determinants of the diagonal blocks. The determinant of a block lower triangular or block upper triangular matrix can be computed similarly.

For instance, consider the following matrix:

$$
\left[
	{\begin{array}{cccc}3 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 5 & - 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 5 & 1 & 1\end{array}}
	\right]
$$

Notice that our matrix is block lower triangular. Therefore, we can compute its determinant as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}3 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 5 & -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 5 & 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} & =\begin{vmatrix}3 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 5 & -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 5 & 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 5 & -1\end{vmatrix}\cdot \begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(-3)\cdot 2 \\  & =-6\end{aligned}
$$
